incompetent

in-KOM-pih-tent — starts with 'in-' (not); an incompetent worker is simply not competent. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Incompetent is lacking the skill or ability needed to do something properly.

The new intern was so incompetent at filing paperwork that half the folders ended up in the wrong drawers.

Example

An incompetent plumber is hired to fix a leaky pipe but ends up flooding the entire kitchen, then leaves without cleaning up or explaining what went wrong.

He couldn't properly perform even a basic task, and he made things worse instead. Unlike 'unlucky,' which implies bad fortune, incompetent means genuinely lacking the necessary skill.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unskilled: Unskilled means without training or practiced ability, and it carries little blame: everyone is unskilled at a job they have never learned. Incompetent is a harsh judgment; it means failing at the very task you were trained and expected to do properly.

unqualified: Unqualified means missing the required credentials, training, or certificates on paper, the licenses and diplomas a job demands. Incompetent is about performance rather than paperwork: a worker can hold every required credential and still prove incompetent at the actual work.

incapable: Incapable means simply not able to do something, for whatever reason; a toddler is incapable of driving a car. Incompetent is narrower and more critical: it describes someone who holds a role or duty and lacks the skill to perform it properly.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

competent: having the necessary skill or ability

skilled: having ability or expertise gained through training

Where it sits · how badly the skill falls short — unpolished → incompetent → inept

unpolished vs. incompetent: Unpolished is weaker than incompetent — someone unpolished just needs more practice, while incompetent means genuinely lacking the ability to do the job at all.

inept vs. incompetent: Inept can feel even sharper than incompetent in tone: both describe a lack of skill, but inept often carries a stronger note of clumsiness or embarrassment.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

prefix — com-

prefix — com-: together (Latin)

root — -pet-

root — -pet-: to seek, to aim at (Latin)

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: adjective-forming (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin competere combined com- (together) with petere (to seek, to aim at) to mean 'to be fit, to coincide.' Adding in- (not) gives incompetent: someone who does not have what it takes to properly aim at and reach the goal.

Use the root in a new word: petition

Use the root in a new word: petition: Neighbors signed a petition asking the city to seek repairs for the broken streetlight.
